sections.h2: What is an Iowa sheriff sale and who runs it?
sections.html:
An Iowa sheriff sale is the public auction of a property after a court has ordered it sold to pay a debt, and the county sheriff conducts it. For a home loan, the road to that auction runs through the district court, because Iowa mortgages can be foreclosed only by a court action in equity, with one narrow exception for a voluntary agreement (Iowa Code chapter 654).

The court enters judgment for the full amount due and orders the property sold as needed to satisfy it. The sale is then made under a special execution. Whether the former owner gets a redemption period afterward depends on which kind of foreclosure the lender chose, which is covered below.

Judgments from other creditors can also end in a sheriff sale, because Iowa enforces money judgments by execution against real estate. Chapter 626 sets the notice and auction rules for both situations, so the steps below apply whichever debt started the case.

sections.h2: What has to happen before the sheriff can sell an Iowa home?
sections.html:
Before a lender files, Iowa requires specific notices, and they differ depending on the property. A skipped notice is often the first thing an owner or attorney checks.

  • One- and two-family residences: a written notice of the right to cure, with thirty days from the notice to bring the loan current, and no acceleration until that time passes (section 654.2D). There is no cure right if a proper notice was given for a default within the previous 365 days.
  • Farmland: a notice of right to cure and a 45-day wait before enforcement (section 654.2A). For farm debt of $20,000 or more, a mediation release is generally needed first (sections 654.2C and 654A.11).
  • Owner-occupied homes: the lender must tell the owner about counseling and mediation on a form the attorney general prescribes, and must give a fourteen-day demand for payment of the accelerated balance to qualify for attorney fees (section 654.4B).

If the court finds the counseling notice was never served and the owner asks for counseling or mediation, the sale can be delayed. That delay cannot exceed sixty days under section 654.4B.

sections.h2: How much notice does an Iowa sheriff sale get?
sections.html:
Real estate sold by a sheriff needs four weeks of notice, posted and published. The table gathers the main timing rules in one place.

RuleWhat the statute saysSection
Notice periodFour weeks before the sale626.74
PostingAt least three public places in the county, one of them the courthouse626.75
NewspaperFirst publication at least four weeks before the sale626.75
Occupying debtorWritten notice served at least twenty days before the sale626.78
Hours of the auctionBetween 9:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m.626.80
Junior creditor requestProof of service filed at least ten days before the sale654.15A

A sheriff who sells without the required notice forfeits $100 to the defendant plus actual damages, but the sale itself stays valid (section 626.77). A sale made without the twenty-day notice to an occupying debtor can be set aside on motion within ninety days (section 626.79). The statutes are on the Iowa Legislature site.

sections.h2: How does the auction itself work?
sections.html:
The sheriff sells at public auction between 9:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m., and the start time and place must appear in the notice. The statute names no single location, so the notice is the only reliable place to find it.

Sealed written bids are allowed. The sheriff receipts them, keeps them sealed until the auction begins, then opens and announces them. If a winning written bidder does not pay in certified funds as the notice directs, the bid is canceled and the sheriff certifies the next highest bidder, within 24 hours for an electronic transfer or 48 hours otherwise (section 626.80).

The sale can be postponed. The sheriff may do so when there are no bidders, when the offer is grossly inadequate, when the judgment creditor asks, or when the parties agree. Without a written agreement, no more than two adjournments of up to sixty days each are allowed (section 626.81).

Two more details matter to owners. A debtor can deliver a signed plan of division before 9:00 a.m. on the sale day so that only the land needed to cover the debt is sold (section 626.84). And any money left after the debt and costs goes to the debtor, unless another execution or valid lien claims it (section 626.82).

sections.h2: How long can an owner redeem after an Iowa sheriff sale?
sections.html:
The default is one year from the day of sale, and the owner keeps possession during that time. The first six months belong to the debtor alone (section 628.3). If the debtor does not redeem, a mortgagee or qualifying creditor may redeem within nine months of the sale (section 628.5).

Shorter periods apply in several situations, so the table is worth checking against the court papers.

SituationRedemption periodSection
Standard saleOne year; debtor alone for six months628.3
Mortgage under 10 acres, if the mortgage provides and the lender waives a deficiencySix months, or three months if not agricultural628.26
Under 10 acres, abandoned, mortgage provides, deficiency waivedSixty days628.27
Non-agricultural, non-residential property180 days; 90 days with a deficiency waiver628.28
Former one- or two-family residence the debtor no longer occupies30 days, or 60 with junior creditors628.28
Foreclosure without redemption elected by the plaintiffNone after the sale654.23

Redeeming a sold home frees it from liability for any unpaid judgment balance (section 628.3). Because the periods differ so much, the dates in the decree and the sheriff's certificate control, not a general rule of thumb.

sections.h2: What is foreclosure without redemption in Iowa?
sections.html:
It is an election the plaintiff can make, on property not used for agriculture, to skip the post-sale redemption period (sections 654.20 through 654.23). The petition has to carry a required notice on its first page.

The owner can answer by filing a demand to delay the sale before judgment. The sale then comes two months after judgment, or six months for a one- or two-family residence, or three months if the petition waives a deficiency judgment (section 654.21). With no demand, the sale is held promptly after judgment.

Once the sale happens, the mortgagor has no right to redeem, and junior lienholders lose theirs too. When someone other than the mortgagee buys, junior liens are extinguished (section 654.23). For a one- or two-family residence with no deficiency waiver and no demand for delay, the plaintiff cannot seek a deficiency judgment (section 654.26).

sections.h2: What happens to the people living in the house?
sections.html:
The owner stays in the home through the redemption period, but once it ends and a deed issues, the former owner can be removed by a court order. A defendant who stays in possession after a foreclosure or execution sale is subject to forcible entry and detainer, unless that person claims paramount title (section 648.1).

  • Written notice to quit: three days before suing (section 648.3).
  • Hearing: set no later than 8 days from filing, or 15 if the plaintiff asks or agrees to a later date (section 648.5).
  • Removal: the execution issues within 3 days of judgment and can be carried out only in the daytime (sections 648.20 and 648.22).

The removal steps run on short clocks, so an owner who wants to choose how the house changes hands has the most room before the sale date.

sections.h2: Can I sell an Iowa house before the sheriff sale?
sections.html:
An owner can generally sell to a buyer at any point before the auction, as long as the sale pays off what the judgment and liens require. A sale closing before the auction can end the case without a sheriff's deed.

Iowa law offers a few related paths. During a pending foreclosure, the plaintiff may ask the court to approve a commercially reasonable sale free of liens, with net proceeds held in escrow (section 654.17A). Before a sheriff's deed is recorded, the judgment creditor may rescind the foreclosure by filing a notice and a $50 fee (section 654.17). A voluntary nonjudicial foreclosure under section 654.18 needs a written agreement from both sides, and the mortgagor gets a five-business-day right to cancel.

The seller of a house in Iowa is liable for the state transfer tax, which is 80 cents for each $500 of value above the first $500 (sections 428A.1 and 428A.3). Cash Home Buyers can look at an Iowa house as-is while the foreclosure is still pending, and you decide whether the numbers work. Talk with an Iowa attorney about your own case first, because the dates in your decree are what count.

faqs.q: Who runs an Iowa sheriff sale?
faqs.a: The sheriff of the county where the property sits runs it. The sale follows a court judgment, and the notice sets the date, start time and place.

faqs.q: How many weeks of notice does Iowa require for a sheriff sale?
faqs.a: Four weeks. The notice must be posted in at least three public places in the county, including the courthouse, and published in a newspaper with the first run at least four weeks before the sale.

faqs.q: Can the owner stay in the house after the sheriff sale?
faqs.a: Usually yes, during the redemption period. The debtor keeps possession while redemption is open, though the period can be as short as 30 days in some cases and nonexistent when foreclosure without redemption was elected.

faqs.q: Is there a deficiency judgment after an Iowa foreclosure?
faqs.a: Sometimes. If the sale does not cover the judgment, a general execution may issue against the mortgagor unless the parties agreed otherwise, but a one- or two-family residence with no deficiency waiver and no demand for delay is protected from a deficiency (sections 654.6 and 654.26).

faqs.q: Can a sheriff sale be postponed?
faqs.a: Yes. The sheriff can postpone for no bidders, a grossly inadequate offer, or a request from the judgment creditor. Without written agreement, two adjournments of up to sixty days each is the limit.
